newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish history mired in sectarian conflict.
newsitem.headline: Irish history mired in sectarian conflict.

text.p: Irish history is mired in rivalry between Protestant and Catholic and conflicting claims of allegiance to governments in London and Dublin.
Following is a guide to the main points and key groups:
NORTHERN IRELAND - was formed when Britain granted home rule to its former Irish colony but partitioned off six counties in the North as a homeland for a predominantly Protestant people.

The Protestants, many of them descendants of Scottish presbyterians who were sent to settle Ireland and stifle the Roman Catholicism of its native people, saw London as their government and the British monarcy as their ruler.
The Catholic minority was harshly treated by the dominant Unionist politicians, so-called because they wanted to preserve 300-year-old union with Britain.

IRELAND - The Irish government accepted the partition of Ireland as the price to be paid for independence but this led to a civil war between those who accepted the founding treaty and others who wanted it to include the "lost" six counties.

The Irish constitution lays claim to Northern Ireland and its people as Irish. This claim has not been altered but successive Dublin governments have pledged to do so to underpin peace and reassure nervous Northern Protestants.
SINN FEIN - was the party that fought for the independence of Ireland. Its guerrilla wing is the Irish Republican Army (IRA).

The IRA has bombed the British mainland regularly in its quest for a united Ireland. In the late 1960s a civil rights movement erupted demanding better treatment for Northern Ireland's Catholics and invigorating republican feelings.
Sinn Fein's constitution says the party opposes violence -- including that of the British army and Protestant RUC police -- but understands those who resort to arms to end colonial rule.
In the mid-1980s it embarked on a "peace strategy" aimed at securing a settlement to match its goal of a United Ireland.

This tempted the IRA to declare a ceasefire in September 1994 in the hope of getting Sinn Fein to the conference table, a goal offered in the December 1993 Downing Street Declaration by Britain and Ireland, the governments' joint peace plan.
This said that Britain would not stand in the way of a united Ireland if a majority in Northern Ireland people wanted it. It also said there would be all-party talks if violence ended.
Sinn Fein enjoys around 10 percent of the popular vote. The IRA ended its truce in February with a series of bombs in mainland Britain.
LOYALISTS - Protestant extremists took to arms seven decades ago to win and maintain their partitioned state. They are called Loyalists because they pledge allegiance to the British crown.
The core group is the Ulster Defence Association, which was banned by the British government.

Two guerrilla groups, the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF) and Ulster Freedom Fighters (UFF), carried out a series of horrific killings of Catholics to terrorise the community from which the IRA and Sinn Fein draw support.

Its political arms, the Ulster Democratic Party (UDP) and Progressive Unionist Party (PUP), have no elected political representatives but say they are the enlightened face of Unionism. Loyalists declared a ceasefire in October 1994 and this still holds. But Loyalist prisoners stated last month they no longer have faith in the peace process.

UNIONISTS - There are a total of 13 Unionists in the British parliament where they defend what they see as an attempt by Britain to reunite Northern Ireland and Ireland under the guise of a peace process.

They draw support from the 60 percent Protestant majority and are crucial to the continuing survival of Prime Minister John Major's Conservative government which has a majority of just one in the 651-seat government.

Unionists believe there is no foundation in law for any attempt to forge closer links between Britain and Ireland, the declared aim of the Anglo-Irish peace process. They see Dublin's involvement as interference in British affairs which masks a desire to carry out the Dublin constitution's claims.

The mainstream Ulster Unionist Party (UUP) is led by David Trimble, who advocated bringing Sinn Fein into the political mainstream through elections to a non-executive assembly. It has nine seats in the London parliament.

The Reverend Ian Paisley's Democratic Unionist Party (DUP has three seats and is to the far right of the UUP. Paisley sees Dublin as "godless" and has called the Vatican anti-Christ. One other Unionist, Robert McCartney, also sits as an MP.

SLDLP - The Social Democratic and Labour party of John Hume is the moderate and legal voice of Irish nationalism. Hume and Adams worked out a still-secret "peace strategy" which preceded the Anglo-Irish Downing Street Declaration.

ALLIANCE PARTY - This small middle of the road group led by John Alderdice has no elected representative but is seen by the British government as an example of the kind of non-sectarian party it would like to encourage.
